**Author: Fanack Water Editorial Team**
Jordan faces one of the world’s most acute water crises. Citizens in the capital Amman sometimes wait a week between water deliveries. Farmers watch their fields dry up. The country has less than 100 cubic meters of freshwater per person annually—far below the United Nations threshold for severe water scarcity. But a transformative megaproject under construction could change this reality by the end of the decade.
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project represents the largest infrastructure undertaking in Jordanian history. A consortium led by French engineering firms Meridiam and Suez, alongside France’s Vinci Construction and Egypt’s Orascom Construction, signed a 30-year concession agreement in January 2025 to design, build, finance, operate, maintain, and eventually transfer the project to the government. The €4 billion initiative (approximately $6 billion USD) promises to deliver 300 million cubic meters of desalinated water annually—enough to supply 40% of Jordan’s drinking water needs.
texts.1:
### **How the Project Works**
The system combines three major components working in tandem. A massive reverse osmosis desalination plant at Aqaba on the Red Sea will produce 851,000 cubic meters of potable water per day—making it the world’s second-largest desalination facility. This water then travels through a 450-kilometer pipeline running northward across Jordanian desert terrain to Amman and surrounding regions, gaining altitude of more than 1,000 meters along the way.
To power this ambitious undertaking, five high-capacity pumping stations will lift the water uphill, while a 281-megawatt solar farm in the Al-Quweira region will supply roughly 28% of the project’s energy needs. This renewable energy component reflects a global shift toward sustainable desalination, with research showing that solar-powered reverse osmosis reduces environmental impact by up to 91% compared to fossil fuel-based systems.
texts.2:
### **Environmental Safeguards Built In**
One common concern with seawater desalination involves brine discharge and its effects on marine ecosystems. The Aqaba project addresses this directly through two targeted measures. The plant uses a special deep-water intake system to avoid coral reef larvae, and deploys a high-velocity brine discharge system that ensures salt concentrations return to normal levels within 20 to 50 meters of the outlet. These design choices reflect lessons learned from decades of desalination experience worldwide.
The project also strategically expands existing water storage facilities at Abu Alandra and Al Muntazah to accommodate the increased supply. Over time, this new desalinated water source will allow Jordan to reduce its dependence on the Disi aquifer—a stressed groundwater reserve that the country has tapped since 2013. This shift protects Jordan’s underground water reserves for future generations.
texts.3:
### **A Lifeline for 3 Million People**
Jordan’s 11 million residents will feel the impact of this project acutely. Once operational by 2029, the system will provide continuous, 24/7 water supply to more than 3 million people in and around Amman—ending the rationing that currently defines life for many Jordanians. For families and businesses that have adapted their schedules around water delivery days, this represents genuine transformation.
The economic implications extend beyond households. Agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of Jordan’s water demand, and reliable freshwater access could stabilize rural livelihoods and food security. Industrial sectors dependent on consistent water supplies will gain predictability for long-term planning and investment.
texts.4:
### **International Financing and Political Backing**
Financing came through in early 2026, a critical milestone for moving the project forward. The Green Climate Fund committed a record $6 billion package—its largest single investment to date—signaling the international community’s recognition of water security as a climate adaptation priority. Beyond the GCF, funding also flows from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the International Finance Corporation, and bilateral grants and loans from multiple countries.
The Meridiam-Suez consortium is providing 15% of project costs through private equity, demonstrating confidence in the venture’s viability. This public-private partnership model distributes risk across multiple stakeholders while ensuring professional management over the 30-year operating period.
texts.5:
### **Broader Implications for the Middle East**
Water experts view the Aqaba-Amman project as a regional test case for how Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) nations can adapt to water stress while prioritizing sustainability. Unlike older desalination initiatives focused purely on water production, this project integrates renewable energy, environmental safeguards, job creation, and climate resilience from the outset.
As rapid urbanization and climate change intensify water scarcity across the region, successful completion of Jordan’s megaproject could inform similar initiatives elsewhere. The combination of advanced technology, international financing mechanisms, and environmental stewardship offers a template for countries facing comparable crises.
texts.6:
### **The Road Ahead**
Construction is already underway, with the target completion date set for 2029. While the technical complexity of moving water across hundreds of kilometers in harsh desert terrain presents significant challenges, the international backing and experienced consortium give the project strong momentum. For a nation where water scarcity has shaped history, geography, and politics for generations, this infrastructure initiative represents genuine hope—and a tangible step toward lasting water security.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
As one of the world’s most water-stressed countries, Jordan faces severe shortages worsened by drought, population growth, and climate change. The country has implemented multiple critical water and wastewater system upgrades to enhance reliability, strengthen resilience, and protect public health.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Delivering reliable potable water
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project now provides desalinated water to millions of Jordanians.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Water reuse at work
The new plant’s wastewater serves as an alternative source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, boosting economic vitality.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Improving energy efficiency
Enhancements saved $11M, cut 85M kWh in power usage, and reduced CO₂ emissions, making supply more sustainable.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Safeguarding for the future
Teams limited greenhouse gas emissions by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.
Beginning in 1992, the U.S. Department of State and CDM Smith collaborated to advance Jordan’s water security through long-term, sustainable solutions. These projects are improving access to clean water, reducing environmental impacts, and ensuring resilient infrastructure that supports the nation’s growth and public health for decades to come.

## Desalination to supply Amman
One of the most significant elements to Jordan’s water trans­for­ma­tion is the Aqaba Amman Water Desali­na­tion and Conveyance Project. Desalinated sea water from the Gulf of Aqaba will be treated at a 300 MCM per year capacity plant featuring a 450 kilometer conveyance system. The project will supply Amman and gover­norates along the conveyance route with 250 million cubic meters (MCM) per year, with the remaining 50 MCM per year planned for Aqaba and the south Wadi Araba area.
To support the Ministry of Water and Irrigation with the planning and procurement of the project, CDM Smith has provided technical, financial, and legal services as the U.S. Department of State's imple­ment­ing partner for this build-operate-transfer 30-year concession contract. In support of this effort, CDM Smith prepared a concept design and feasibility cost estimate to determine the viability and bankability of treating seawater and a conveyance system from Aqaba to Amman. The project has also taken on climate change priorities to limit greenhouse gas emissions from the power consumption by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.

## Sanitation for Aqaba's growing population
The North Aqaba Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) is another upgrade completed under the U.S. Department of State. Originally constructed in 1986 with enough capacity to receive 9,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day, Aqaba Water Company expanded and reha­bil­i­tated the plant in 2021 to accommodate the sanitation needs of Aqaba’s growing population and to enhance sanitation services for residents of the Aqaba Governorate. CDM Smith supported the construc­tion of the new facilities and the reha­bil­i­ta­tion of the existing wastewater treatment plant. The new expansion can accommodate an extra 28,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day—40,000 cubic meters in total. The plant now has enough capacity to safely manage sanitation services for 150,000 people in the Aqaba Governorate.
The new facility includes a combination of solar power and biogas produced through the wastewater treatment process. These green alter­na­tives are elevating the plant’s ability to meet energy demands of the new expansion, including the energy needed to pump treated water for reuse. By preventing the cont­a­m­i­na­tion of Jordan’s precious freshwater sources, this initiative is protecting public health and envi­ron­men­tal standards while lowering operating costs.

## Upgrading the Tafileh WWTP
The U.S. Department of State, the Government of Jordan, and CDM Smith also made strides to accommodate the sanitation needs of Tafileh’s growing population by replacing the existing Tafileh WWTP with a higher-capacity, more efficient plant for residents of the Tafileh Governorate. The original WWTP was constructed in 1989 with enough capacity to receive 1,600 cubic meters of wastewater per day, but the new plant has allowed for waste processing capacity of 5,000 cubic meters per day with the potential to expand to 7,500 cubic meters per day. The new plant’s capacity tripled from about 25,000 to over 78,000 people. This treated wastewater serves as an alternative water source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, allowing potable surface and groundwater sources to be used for drinking.

## Providing freshwater wells in Dair Alla
CDM Smith is also supporting U.S. Department of State's Water and Wastewater Improvement Efforts for Dair Alla, a district in Balqa Governorate in the Jordan Valley with no wastewater pipeline networks, by providing well drilling contract tender evaluation and pre-contract services. To increase the availability of much-needed fresh water, the team is rehabilitating groundwater wells, upgrading a desalination water treatment plant and building a water transmission system serving 17 localities. These additions to Dair Alla will allow for an influx of fresh water available, keeping pace with the growing demand driven by population increases.

**Author: Fanack Water Editorial Team**
Jordan faces one of the world’s most acute water crises. Citizens in the capital Amman sometimes wait a week between water deliveries. Farmers watch their fields dry up. The country has less than 100 cubic meters of freshwater per person annually—far below the United Nations threshold for severe water scarcity. But a transformative megaproject under construction could change this reality by the end of the decade.
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project represents the largest infrastructure undertaking in Jordanian history. A consortium led by French engineering firms Meridiam and Suez, alongside France’s Vinci Construction and Egypt’s Orascom Construction, signed a 30-year concession agreement in January 2025 to design, build, finance, operate, maintain, and eventually transfer the project to the government. The €4 billion initiative (approximately $6 billion USD) promises to deliver 300 million cubic meters of desalinated water annually—enough to supply 40% of Jordan’s drinking water needs.

### **How the Project Works**
The system combines three major components working in tandem. A massive reverse osmosis desalination plant at Aqaba on the Red Sea will produce 851,000 cubic meters of potable water per day—making it the world’s second-largest desalination facility. This water then travels through a 450-kilometer pipeline running northward across Jordanian desert terrain to Amman and surrounding regions, gaining altitude of more than 1,000 meters along the way.
To power this ambitious undertaking, five high-capacity pumping stations will lift the water uphill, while a 281-megawatt solar farm in the Al-Quweira region will supply roughly 28% of the project’s energy needs. This renewable energy component reflects a global shift toward sustainable desalination, with research showing that solar-powered reverse osmosis reduces environmental impact by up to 91% compared to fossil fuel-based systems.

### **Environmental Safeguards Built In**
One common concern with seawater desalination involves brine discharge and its effects on marine ecosystems. The Aqaba project addresses this directly through two targeted measures. The plant uses a special deep-water intake system to avoid coral reef larvae, and deploys a high-velocity brine discharge system that ensures salt concentrations return to normal levels within 20 to 50 meters of the outlet. These design choices reflect lessons learned from decades of desalination experience worldwide.
The project also strategically expands existing water storage facilities at Abu Alandra and Al Muntazah to accommodate the increased supply. Over time, this new desalinated water source will allow Jordan to reduce its dependence on the Disi aquifer—a stressed groundwater reserve that the country has tapped since 2013. This shift protects Jordan’s underground water reserves for future generations.

### **A Lifeline for 3 Million People**
Jordan’s 11 million residents will feel the impact of this project acutely. Once operational by 2029, the system will provide continuous, 24/7 water supply to more than 3 million people in and around Amman—ending the rationing that currently defines life for many Jordanians. For families and businesses that have adapted their schedules around water delivery days, this represents genuine transformation.
The economic implications extend beyond households. Agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of Jordan’s water demand, and reliable freshwater access could stabilize rural livelihoods and food security. Industrial sectors dependent on consistent water supplies will gain predictability for long-term planning and investment.

### **International Financing and Political Backing**
Financing came through in early 2026, a critical milestone for moving the project forward. The Green Climate Fund committed a record $6 billion package—its largest single investment to date—signaling the international community’s recognition of water security as a climate adaptation priority. Beyond the GCF, funding also flows from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the International Finance Corporation, and bilateral grants and loans from multiple countries.
The Meridiam-Suez consortium is providing 15% of project costs through private equity, demonstrating confidence in the venture’s viability. This public-private partnership model distributes risk across multiple stakeholders while ensuring professional management over the 30-year operating period.

### **Broader Implications for the Middle East**
Water experts view the Aqaba-Amman project as a regional test case for how Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) nations can adapt to water stress while prioritizing sustainability. Unlike older desalination initiatives focused purely on water production, this project integrates renewable energy, environmental safeguards, job creation, and climate resilience from the outset.
As rapid urbanization and climate change intensify water scarcity across the region, successful completion of Jordan’s megaproject could inform similar initiatives elsewhere. The combination of advanced technology, international financing mechanisms, and environmental stewardship offers a template for countries facing comparable crises.

### **The Road Ahead**
Construction is already underway, with the target completion date set for 2029. While the technical complexity of moving water across hundreds of kilometers in harsh desert terrain presents significant challenges, the international backing and experienced consortium give the project strong momentum. For a nation where water scarcity has shaped history, geography, and politics for generations, this infrastructure initiative represents genuine hope—and a tangible step toward lasting water security.

Title: Jordan’s first SWRO opens for business
Chunks: 0,1,2
The opening of the first seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) plant in Jordan marks a jumping off point for the country from which it can continue to develop a desalination programme, including the much-anticipated Red Sea-Dead Sea project.

### The SWRO plant is purifying high salinity waters
*   Gulf of Aqaba is a semi-closed and high salinity body of water  
*   Plant uses cooling outtake water from KEMAPCO fertiliser business as its intake water  
*   Jordan’s first RO plant blazes a trail for the technology within the country
The first seawater desalination plant in Jordan, in the Gulf of Aqaba, began production in April 2017. Jordanian water treatment company AquaTreat, which has previously delivered seawater desalination projects for oil companies in the Arabian Gulf, provided all engineering, construction, and technology. The plant uses a conventional system of microfiltration, ultrafiltration, and reverse osmosis (MF-UF-RO), and has capacity of 15,000 m3/d.
Water utility Aqaba Water Company buys 70 per cent of the desalinated water, and Arab Fertilisers & Chemicals Industries (KEMAPCO) takes 30 per cent. The facility uses the cooling water outtake from KEMAPCO’s process as its intake water, and returns the RO brine to the fertiliser company’s drain. “It is seawater, it’s three degrees warmer, plus it’s chlorinated. KEMAPCO does its own screening on its intake, and they chlorinate it,” says Tarek Dehays AquaTreat chief executive.
“The Gulf of Aqaba is a closed gulf in a way. The salinity of the water is higher than normal open water, so we’re reaching 40,000 to 44,000 parts per million (PPM) intake. Our RO output is less than 200 — after lime addition and post treatment we’re reaching 210 to 220 PPM. The plant uses electricity from the grid. (An official report initially said it used methane and solar, but had mixed up the matter with details of a wastewater treatment project in the north of Aqaba.) It’s a seven-year build, operate, transfer contract.

### Project paves the way for future developments
*   Developers of tourist villages are pushing for permission for desalination plants  
*   Data from the AquaTreat plant could provide insight to the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project  
*   Country’s first RO plant is a “self-affirmation” of capability
Water supplies in Jordan have come under increasing pressure, particularly from large numbers of refugees arriving from Syria over the past six years. Now that the Aqaba project has nudged open the door, developers may find it easier to push ahead with future desalination projects in the country, whether for drinking and sanitation for local populations, or for business and industry. One area of demand is from property developers that want to build tourist complexes, and are seeking permission from the government for desalination facilities.
The other development on the horizon is the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project, a major infrastructure scheme that will help to protect the Dead Sea environment and to boost water supply for Israel, Jordan, and Palestine. The proposal is for a 220,000 m3/d SWRO desalination plant on the Gulf of Aqaba, whose brine will be piped 180 kilometres across the country to replenish the Dead Sea. Jordan and Israel have raised $400 million towards the conveyance aspect; and the remainder of the estimated $1billion project cost will be met by private finance.
AquaTreat’s project can be seen a positive step towards realising the Red-Dead project, because it puts down a marker for desalination technology in Jordan. “Whatever technical information is coming out is going to be important for the country, because it’s the first trial for desalinated water in the Gulf of Aqaba, which is a very sensitive ecosystem, a very closed gulf. It’s at the end of the Red Sea, so it’s a very, very particular kind of water from a technical point of view, and it will be very interesting for everybody to see the output, and how can this water be dealt with, and what problems might arise over time,” Tarek says. “Jordan now has its own desalination plant, Jordanian built, Jordanian consumed. This is a self-affirmation that we can do it.”

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
As one of the world’s most water-stressed countries, Jordan faces severe shortages worsened by drought, population growth, and climate change. The country has implemented multiple critical water and wastewater system upgrades to enhance reliability, strengthen resilience, and protect public health.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Delivering reliable potable water
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project now provides desalinated water to millions of Jordanians.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Water reuse at work
The new plant’s wastewater serves as an alternative source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, boosting economic vitality.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Improving energy efficiency
Enhancements saved $11M, cut 85M kWh in power usage, and reduced CO₂ emissions, making supply more sustainable.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Safeguarding for the future
Teams limited greenhouse gas emissions by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.
Beginning in 1992, the U.S. Department of State and CDM Smith collaborated to advance Jordan’s water security through long-term, sustainable solutions. These projects are improving access to clean water, reducing environmental impacts, and ensuring resilient infrastructure that supports the nation’s growth and public health for decades to come.

## Desalination to supply Amman
One of the most significant elements to Jordan’s water trans­for­ma­tion is the Aqaba Amman Water Desali­na­tion and Conveyance Project. Desalinated sea water from the Gulf of Aqaba will be treated at a 300 MCM per year capacity plant featuring a 450 kilometer conveyance system. The project will supply Amman and gover­norates along the conveyance route with 250 million cubic meters (MCM) per year, with the remaining 50 MCM per year planned for Aqaba and the south Wadi Araba area.
To support the Ministry of Water and Irrigation with the planning and procurement of the project, CDM Smith has provided technical, financial, and legal services as the U.S. Department of State's imple­ment­ing partner for this build-operate-transfer 30-year concession contract. In support of this effort, CDM Smith prepared a concept design and feasibility cost estimate to determine the viability and bankability of treating seawater and a conveyance system from Aqaba to Amman. The project has also taken on climate change priorities to limit greenhouse gas emissions from the power consumption by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.

## Sanitation for Aqaba's growing population
The North Aqaba Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) is another upgrade completed under the U.S. Department of State. Originally constructed in 1986 with enough capacity to receive 9,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day, Aqaba Water Company expanded and reha­bil­i­tated the plant in 2021 to accommodate the sanitation needs of Aqaba’s growing population and to enhance sanitation services for residents of the Aqaba Governorate. CDM Smith supported the construc­tion of the new facilities and the reha­bil­i­ta­tion of the existing wastewater treatment plant. The new expansion can accommodate an extra 28,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day—40,000 cubic meters in total. The plant now has enough capacity to safely manage sanitation services for 150,000 people in the Aqaba Governorate.
The new facility includes a combination of solar power and biogas produced through the wastewater treatment process. These green alter­na­tives are elevating the plant’s ability to meet energy demands of the new expansion, including the energy needed to pump treated water for reuse. By preventing the cont­a­m­i­na­tion of Jordan’s precious freshwater sources, this initiative is protecting public health and envi­ron­men­tal standards while lowering operating costs.

## Upgrading the Tafileh WWTP
The U.S. Department of State, the Government of Jordan, and CDM Smith also made strides to accommodate the sanitation needs of Tafileh’s growing population by replacing the existing Tafileh WWTP with a higher-capacity, more efficient plant for residents of the Tafileh Governorate. The original WWTP was constructed in 1989 with enough capacity to receive 1,600 cubic meters of wastewater per day, but the new plant has allowed for waste processing capacity of 5,000 cubic meters per day with the potential to expand to 7,500 cubic meters per day. The new plant’s capacity tripled from about 25,000 to over 78,000 people. This treated wastewater serves as an alternative water source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, allowing potable surface and groundwater sources to be used for drinking.

## Providing freshwater wells in Dair Alla
CDM Smith is also supporting U.S. Department of State's Water and Wastewater Improvement Efforts for Dair Alla, a district in Balqa Governorate in the Jordan Valley with no wastewater pipeline networks, by providing well drilling contract tender evaluation and pre-contract services. These additions to Dair Alla will allow for an influx of fresh water available, keeping pace with the growing demand driven by population increases.

texts.0: The opening of the first seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) plant in Jordan marks a jumping off point for the country from which it can continue to develop a desalination programme, including the much-anticipated Red Sea-Dead Sea project.
texts.1:
### The SWRO plant is purifying high salinity waters
*   Gulf of Aqaba is a semi-closed and high salinity body of water  
*   Plant uses cooling outtake water from KEMAPCO fertiliser business as its intake water  
*   Jordan’s first RO plant blazes a trail for the technology within the country
The first seawater desalination plant in Jordan, in the Gulf of Aqaba, began production in April 2017. Jordanian water treatment company AquaTreat, which has previously delivered seawater desalination projects for oil companies in the Arabian Gulf, provided all engineering, construction, and technology. The plant uses a conventional system of microfiltration, ultrafiltration, and reverse osmosis (MF-UF-RO), and has capacity of 15,000 m3/d.
Water utility Aqaba Water Company buys 70 per cent of the desalinated water, and Arab Fertilisers & Chemicals Industries (KEMAPCO) takes 30 per cent. The facility uses the cooling water outtake from KEMAPCO’s process as its intake water, and returns the RO brine to the fertiliser company’s drain. “It is seawater, it’s three degrees warmer, plus it’s chlorinated. KEMAPCO does its own screening on its intake, and they chlorinate it,” says Tarek Dehays AquaTreat chief executive.
“The Gulf of Aqaba is a closed gulf in a way. The salinity of the water is higher than normal open water, so we’re reaching 40,000 to 44,000 parts per million (PPM) intake. Our RO output is less than 200 — after lime addition and post treatment we’re reaching 210 to 220 PPM. The plant uses electricity from the grid. (An official report initially said it used methane and solar, but had mixed up the matter with details of a wastewater treatment project in the north of Aqaba.) It’s a seven-year build, operate, transfer contract.
texts.2:
### Project paves the way for future developments
*   Developers of tourist villages are pushing for permission for desalination plants  
*   Data from the AquaTreat plant could provide insight to the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project  
*   Country’s first RO plant is a “self-affirmation” of capability
Water supplies in Jordan have come under increasing pressure, particularly from large numbers of refugees arriving from Syria over the past six years. Now that the Aqaba project has nudged open the door, developers may find it easier to push ahead with future desalination projects in the country, whether for drinking and sanitation for local populations, or for business and industry. One area of demand is from property developers that want to build tourist complexes, and are seeking permission from the government for desalination facilities.
The other development on the horizon is the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project, a major infrastructure scheme that will help to protect the Dead Sea environment and to boost water supply for Israel, Jordan, and Palestine. The proposal is for a 220,000 m3/d SWRO desalination plant on the Gulf of Aqaba, whose brine will be piped 180 kilometres across the country to replenish the Dead Sea. Jordan and Israel have raised $400 million towards the conveyance aspect; and the remainder of the estimated $1billion project cost will be met by private finance.
AquaTreat’s project can be seen a positive step towards realising the Red-Dead project, because it puts down a marker for desalination technology in Jordan. “Whatever technical information is coming out is going to be important for the country, because it’s the first trial for desalinated water in the Gulf of Aqaba, which is a very sensitive ecosystem, a very closed gulf. It’s at the end of the Red Sea, so it’s a very, very particular kind of water from a technical point of view, and it will be very interesting for everybody to see the output, and how can this water be dealt with, and what problems might arise over time,” Tarek says. “Jordan now has its own desalination plant, Jordanian built, Jordanian consumed. This is a self-affirmation that we can do it.”

_Panorama of Amman Cityscape with Huge Flag Hoisted on a Mast, Jordan (AXP Photography)_
**Author: Fanack Water Editorial Team**
Jordan faces one of the world’s most acute water crises. Citizens in the capital Amman sometimes wait a week between water deliveries. Farmers watch their fields dry up. The country has less than 100 cubic meters of freshwater per person annually—far below the United Nations threshold for severe water scarcity. But a transformative megaproject under construction could change this reality by the end of the decade.
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project represents the largest infrastructure undertaking in Jordanian history. A consortium led by French engineering firms Meridiam and Suez, alongside France’s Vinci Construction and Egypt’s Orascom Construction, signed a 30-year concession agreement in January 2025 to design, build, finance, operate, maintain, and eventually transfer the project to the government. The €4 billion initiative (approximately $6 billion USD) promises to deliver 300 million cubic meters of desalinated water annually—enough to supply 40% of Jordan’s drinking water needs.
texts.1:
### **How the Project Works**
The system combines three major components working in tandem. A massive reverse osmosis desalination plant at Aqaba on the Red Sea will produce 851,000 cubic meters of potable water per day—making it the world’s second-largest desalination facility. This water then travels through a 450-kilometer pipeline running northward across Jordanian desert terrain to Amman and surrounding regions, gaining altitude of more than 1,000 meters along the way.
To power this ambitious undertaking, five high-capacity pumping stations will lift the water uphill, while a 281-megawatt solar farm in the Al-Quweira region will supply roughly 28% of the project’s energy needs. This renewable energy component reflects a global shift toward sustainable desalination, with research showing that solar-powered reverse osmosis reduces environmental impact by up to 91% compared to fossil fuel-based systems.
texts.2:
### **Environmental Safeguards Built In**
One common concern with seawater desalination involves brine discharge and its effects on marine ecosystems. The Aqaba project addresses this directly through two targeted measures. The plant uses a special deep-water intake system to avoid coral reef larvae, and deploys a high-velocity brine discharge system that ensures salt concentrations return to normal levels within 20 to 50 meters of the outlet. These design choices reflect lessons learned from decades of desalination experience worldwide.
The project also strategically expands existing water storage facilities at Abu Alandra and Al Muntazah to accommodate the increased supply. Over time, this new desalinated water source will allow Jordan to reduce its dependence on the Disi aquifer—a stressed groundwater reserve that the country has tapped since 2013. This shift protects Jordan’s underground water reserves for future generations.
texts.3:
### **A Lifeline for 3 Million People**
Jordan’s 11 million residents will feel the impact of this project acutely. Once operational by 2029, the system will provide continuous, 24/7 water supply to more than 3 million people in and around Amman—ending the rationing that currently defines life for many Jordanians. For families and businesses that have adapted their schedules around water delivery days, this represents genuine transformation.
The economic implications extend beyond households. Agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of Jordan’s water demand, and reliable freshwater access could stabilize rural livelihoods and food security. Industrial sectors dependent on consistent water supplies will gain predictability for long-term planning and investment.
texts.4:
### **International Financing and Political Backing**
Financing came through in early 2026, a critical milestone for moving the project forward. The Green Climate Fund committed a record $6 billion package—its largest single investment to date—signaling the international community’s recognition of water security as a climate adaptation priority. Beyond the GCF, funding also flows from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the International Finance Corporation, and bilateral grants and loans from multiple countries.
The Meridiam-Suez consortium is providing 15% of project costs through private equity, demonstrating confidence in the venture’s viability. This public-private partnership model distributes risk across multiple stakeholders while ensuring professional management over the 30-year operating period.
texts.5:
### **Broader Implications for the Middle East**
Water experts view the Aqaba-Amman project as a regional test case for how Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) nations can adapt to water stress while prioritizing sustainability. Unlike older desalination initiatives focused purely on water production, this project integrates renewable energy, environmental safeguards, job creation, and climate resilience from the outset.
As rapid urbanization and climate change intensify water scarcity across the region, successful completion of Jordan’s megaproject could inform similar initiatives elsewhere. The combination of advanced technology, international financing mechanisms, and environmental stewardship offers a template for countries facing comparable crises.
texts.6:
### **The Road Ahead**
Construction is already underway, with the target completion date set for 2029. While the technical complexity of moving water across hundreds of kilometers in harsh desert terrain presents significant challenges, the international backing and experienced consortium give the project strong momentum. For a nation where water scarcity has shaped history, geography, and politics for generations, this infrastructure initiative represents genuine hope—and a tangible step toward lasting water security.

texts.0:
## Advancing water security through infrastructure
As one of the world’s most water-stressed countries, Jordan faces severe shortages worsened by drought, population growth, and climate change. The country has implemented multiple critical water and wastewater system upgrades to enhance reliability, strengthen resilience, and protect public health.
texts.1:
## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Delivering reliable potable water
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project now provides desalinated water to millions of Jordanians.
texts.2:
## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Water reuse at work
The new plant’s wastewater serves as an alternative source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, boosting economic vitality.
texts.3:
## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Improving energy efficiency
Enhancements saved $11M, cut 85M kWh in power usage, and reduced CO₂ emissions, making supply more sustainable.
texts.4:
## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Safeguarding for the future
Teams limited greenhouse gas emissions by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.
Beginning in 1992, the U.S. Department of State and CDM Smith collaborated to advance Jordan’s water security through long-term, sustainable solutions. These projects are improving access to clean water, reducing environmental impacts, and ensuring resilient infrastructure that supports the nation’s growth and public health for decades to come.
texts.5:
## Desalination to supply Amman
One of the most significant elements to Jordan’s water trans­for­ma­tion is the Aqaba Amman Water Desali­na­tion and Conveyance Project. Desalinated sea water from the Gulf of Aqaba will be treated at a 300 MCM per year capacity plant featuring a 450 kilometer conveyance system. The project will supply Amman and gover­norates along the conveyance route with 250 million cubic meters (MCM) per year, with the remaining 50 MCM per year planned for Aqaba and the south Wadi Araba area.
To support the Ministry of Water and Irrigation with the planning and procurement of the project, CDM Smith has provided technical, financial, and legal services as the U.S. Department of State's imple­ment­ing partner for this build-operate-transfer 30-year concession contract. In support of this effort, CDM Smith prepared a concept design and feasibility cost estimate to determine the viability and bankability of treating seawater and a conveyance system from Aqaba to Amman. The project has also taken on climate change priorities to limit greenhouse gas emissions from the power consumption by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.
texts.6:
## Sanitation for Aqaba's growing population
The North Aqaba Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) is another upgrade completed under the U.S. Department of State. Originally constructed in 1986 with enough capacity to receive 9,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day, Aqaba Water Company expanded and reha­bil­i­tated the plant in 2021 to accommodate the sanitation needs of Aqaba’s growing population and to enhance sanitation services for residents of the Aqaba Governorate. CDM Smith supported the construc­tion of the new facilities and the reha­bil­i­ta­tion of the existing wastewater treatment plant. The new expansion can accommodate an extra 28,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day—40,000 cubic meters in total. The plant now has enough capacity to safely manage sanitation services for 150,000 people in the Aqaba Governorate.
The new facility includes a combination of solar power and biogas produced through the wastewater treatment process. These green alter­na­tives are elevating the plant’s ability to meet energy demands of the new expansion, including the energy needed to pump treated water for reuse. By preventing the cont­a­m­i­na­tion of Jordan’s precious freshwater sources, this initiative is protecting public health and envi­ron­men­tal standards while lowering operating costs.
texts.7:
## Upgrading the Tafileh WWTP
The U.S. Department of State, the Government of Jordan, and CDM Smith also made strides to accommodate the sanitation needs of Tafileh’s growing population by replacing the existing Tafileh WWTP with a higher-capacity, more efficient plant for residents of the Tafileh Governorate. The original WWTP was constructed in 1989 with enough capacity to receive 1,600 cubic meters of wastewater per day, but the new plant has allowed for waste processing capacity of 5,000 cubic meters per day with the potential to expand to 7,500 cubic meters per day. The new plant’s capacity tripled from about 25,000 to over 78,000 people. This treated wastewater serves as an alternative water source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, allowing potable surface and groundwater sources to be used for drinking.
texts.8:
## Providing freshwater wells in Dair Alla
CDM Smith is also supporting U.S. Department of State's Water and Wastewater Improvement Efforts for Dair Alla, a district in Balqa Governorate in the Jordan Valley with no wastewater pipeline networks, by providing well drilling contract tender evaluation and pre-contract services. To increase the availability of much-needed fresh water, the team is rehabilitating groundwater wells, upgrading a desalination water treatment plant and building a water transmission system serving 17 localities. These additions to Dair Alla will allow for an influx of fresh water available, keeping pace with the growing demand driven by population increases.

### The SWRO plant is purifying high salinity waters
*   Gulf of Aqaba is a semi-closed and high salinity body of water  
*   Plant uses cooling outtake water from KEMAPCO fertiliser business as its intake water  
*   Jordan’s first RO plant blazes a trail for the technology within the country
The first seawater desalination plant in Jordan, in the Gulf of Aqaba, began production in April 2017. Jordanian water treatment company AquaTreat, which has previously delivered seawater desalination projects for oil companies in the Arabian Gulf, provided all engineering, construction, and technology. The plant uses a conventional system of microfiltration, ultrafiltration, and reverse osmosis (MF-UF-RO), and has capacity of 15,000 m3/d.
Water utility Aqaba Water Company buys 70 per cent of the desalinated water, and Arab Fertilisers & Chemicals Industries (KEMAPCO) takes 30 per cent. The facility uses the cooling water outtake from KEMAPCO’s process as its intake water, and returns the RO brine to the fertiliser company’s drain. “It is seawater, it’s three degrees warmer, plus it’s chlorinated. KEMAPCO does its own screening on its intake, and they chlorinate it,” says Tarek Dehays AquaTreat chief executive.
“The Gulf of Aqaba is a closed gulf in a way. The salinity of the water is higher than normal open water, so we’re reaching 40,000 to 44,000 parts per million (PPM) intake. Our RO output is less than 200 — after lime addition and post treatment we’re reaching 210 to 220 PPM. The plant uses electricity from the grid. (An official report initially said it used methane and solar, but had mixed up the matter with details of a wastewater treatment project in the north of Aqaba.) It’s a seven-year build, operate, transfer contract.

### Project paves the way for future developments
*   Developers of tourist villages are pushing for permission for desalination plants  
*   Data from the AquaTreat plant could provide insight to the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project  
*   Country’s first RO plant is a “self-affirmation” of capability
Water supplies in Jordan have come under increasing pressure, particularly from large numbers of refugees arriving from Syria over the past six years. Now that the Aqaba project has nudged open the door, developers may find it easier to push ahead with future desalination projects in the country, whether for drinking and sanitation for local populations, or for business and industry. One area of demand is from property developers that want to build tourist complexes, and are seeking permission from the government for desalination facilities.
The other development on the horizon is the Red Sea-Dead Sea mega project, a major infrastructure scheme that will help to protect the Dead Sea environment and to boost water supply for Israel, Jordan, and Palestine. The proposal is for a 220,000 m3/d SWRO desalination plant on the Gulf of Aqaba, whose brine will be piped 180 kilometres across the country to replenish the Dead Sea. Jordan and Israel have raised $400 million towards the conveyance aspect; and the remainder of the estimated $1billion project cost will be met by private finance.
AquaTreat’s project can be seen a positive step towards realising the Red-Dead project, because it puts down a marker for desalination technology in Jordan. “Whatever technical information is coming out is going to be important for the country, because it’s the first trial for desalinated water in the Gulf of Aqaba, which is a very sensitive ecosystem, a very closed gulf. It’s at the end of the Red Sea, so it’s a very, very particular kind of water from a technical point of view, and it will be very interesting for everybody to see the output, and how can this water be dealt with, and what problems might arise over time,” Tarek says. “Jordan now has its own desalination plant, Jordanian built, Jordanian consumed. This is a self-affirmation that we can do it.”

**Author: Fanack Water Editorial Team**
Jordan faces one of the world’s most acute water crises. Citizens in the capital Amman sometimes wait a week between water deliveries. Farmers watch their fields dry up. The country has less than 100 cubic meters of freshwater per person annually—far below the United Nations threshold for severe water scarcity. But a transformative megaproject under construction could change this reality by the end of the decade.
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project represents the largest infrastructure undertaking in Jordanian history. A consortium led by French engineering firms Meridiam and Suez, alongside France’s Vinci Construction and Egypt’s Orascom Construction, signed a 30-year concession agreement in January 2025 to design, build, finance, operate, maintain, and eventually transfer the project to the government. The €4 billion initiative (approximately $6 billion USD) promises to deliver 300 million cubic meters of desalinated water annually—enough to supply 40% of Jordan’s drinking water needs.

### **How the Project Works**
The system combines three major components working in tandem. A massive reverse osmosis desalination plant at Aqaba on the Red Sea will produce 851,000 cubic meters of potable water per day—making it the world’s second-largest desalination facility. This water then travels through a 450-kilometer pipeline running northward across Jordanian desert terrain to Amman and surrounding regions, gaining altitude of more than 1,000 meters along the way.
To power this ambitious undertaking, five high-capacity pumping stations will lift the water uphill, while a 281-megawatt solar farm in the Al-Quweira region will supply roughly 28% of the project’s energy needs. This renewable energy component reflects a global shift toward sustainable desalination, with research showing that solar-powered reverse osmosis reduces environmental impact by up to 91% compared to fossil fuel-based systems.

### **Environmental Safeguards Built In**
One common concern with seawater desalination involves brine discharge and its effects on marine ecosystems. The Aqaba project addresses this directly through two targeted measures. The plant uses a special deep-water intake system to avoid coral reef larvae, and deploys a high-velocity brine discharge system that ensures salt concentrations return to normal levels within 20 to 50 meters of the outlet. These design choices reflect lessons learned from decades of desalination experience worldwide.
The project also strategically expands existing water storage facilities at Abu Alandra and Al Muntazah to accommodate the increased supply. Over time, this new desalinated water source will allow Jordan to reduce its dependence on the Disi aquifer—a stressed groundwater reserve that the country has tapped since 2013. This shift protects Jordan’s underground water reserves for future generations.

### **A Lifeline for 3 Million People**
Jordan’s 11 million residents will feel the impact of this project acutely. Once operational by 2029, the system will provide continuous, 24/7 water supply to more than 3 million people in and around Amman—ending the rationing that currently defines life for many Jordanians. For families and businesses that have adapted their schedules around water delivery days, this represents genuine transformation.
The economic implications extend beyond households. Agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of Jordan’s water demand, and reliable freshwater access could stabilize rural livelihoods and food security. Industrial sectors dependent on consistent water supplies will gain predictability for long-term planning and investment.

### **International Financing and Political Backing**
Financing came through in early 2026, a critical milestone for moving the project forward. The Green Climate Fund committed a record $6 billion package—its largest single investment to date—signaling the international community’s recognition of water security as a climate adaptation priority. Beyond the GCF, funding also flows from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the International Finance Corporation, and bilateral grants and loans from multiple countries.
The Meridiam-Suez consortium is providing 15% of project costs through private equity, demonstrating confidence in the venture’s viability. This public-private partnership model distributes risk across multiple stakeholders while ensuring professional management over the 30-year operating period.

### **Broader Implications for the Middle East**
Water experts view the Aqaba-Amman project as a regional test case for how Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) nations can adapt to water stress while prioritizing sustainability. Unlike older desalination initiatives focused purely on water production, this project integrates renewable energy, environmental safeguards, job creation, and climate resilience from the outset.
As rapid urbanization and climate change intensify water scarcity across the region, successful completion of Jordan’s megaproject could inform similar initiatives elsewhere. The combination of advanced technology, international financing mechanisms, and environmental stewardship offers a template for countries facing comparable crises.

### **The Road Ahead**
Construction is already underway, with the target completion date set for 2029. While the technical complexity of moving water across hundreds of kilometers in harsh desert terrain presents significant challenges, the international backing and experienced consortium give the project strong momentum. For a nation where water scarcity has shaped history, geography, and politics for generations, this infrastructure initiative represents genuine hope—and a tangible step toward lasting water security.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
As one of the world’s most water-stressed countries, Jordan faces severe shortages worsened by drought, population growth, and climate change. The country has implemented multiple critical water and wastewater system upgrades to enhance reliability, strengthen resilience, and protect public health.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Delivering reliable potable water
The Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project now provides desalinated water to millions of Jordanians.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Water reuse at work
The new plant’s wastewater serves as an alternative source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, boosting economic vitality.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Improving energy efficiency
Enhancements saved $11M, cut 85M kWh in power usage, and reduced CO₂ emissions, making supply more sustainable.

## Advancing water security through infrastructure
### Safeguarding for the future
Teams limited greenhouse gas emissions by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.
Beginning in 1992, the U.S. Department of State and CDM Smith collaborated to advance Jordan’s water security through long-term, sustainable solutions. These projects are improving access to clean water, reducing environmental impacts, and ensuring resilient infrastructure that supports the nation’s growth and public health for decades to come.

## Desalination to supply Amman
One of the most significant elements to Jordan’s water trans­for­ma­tion is the Aqaba Amman Water Desali­na­tion and Conveyance Project. Desalinated sea water from the Gulf of Aqaba will be treated at a 300 MCM per year capacity plant featuring a 450 kilometer conveyance system. The project will supply Amman and gover­norates along the conveyance route with 250 million cubic meters (MCM) per year, with the remaining 50 MCM per year planned for Aqaba and the south Wadi Araba area.
To support the Ministry of Water and Irrigation with the planning and procurement of the project, CDM Smith has provided technical, financial, and legal services as the U.S. Department of State's imple­ment­ing partner for this build-operate-transfer 30-year concession contract. In support of this effort, CDM Smith prepared a concept design and feasibility cost estimate to determine the viability and bankability of treating seawater and a conveyance system from Aqaba to Amman. The project has also taken on climate change priorities to limit greenhouse gas emissions from the power consumption by introducing a renewable energy generation facility as part of the scope.

## Sanitation for Aqaba's growing population
The North Aqaba Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP) is another upgrade completed under the U.S. Department of State. Originally constructed in 1986 with enough capacity to receive 9,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day, Aqaba Water Company expanded and reha­bil­i­tated the plant in 2021 to accommodate the sanitation needs of Aqaba’s growing population and to enhance sanitation services for residents of the Aqaba Governorate. CDM Smith supported the construc­tion of the new facilities and the reha­bil­i­ta­tion of the existing wastewater treatment plant. The new expansion can accommodate an extra 28,000 cubic meters of wastewater per day—40,000 cubic meters in total. The plant now has enough capacity to safely manage sanitation services for 150,000 people in the Aqaba Governorate.
The new facility includes a combination of solar power and biogas produced through the wastewater treatment process. These green alter­na­tives are elevating the plant’s ability to meet energy demands of the new expansion, including the energy needed to pump treated water for reuse. By preventing the cont­a­m­i­na­tion of Jordan’s precious freshwater sources, this initiative is protecting public health and envi­ron­men­tal standards while lowering operating costs.

## Upgrading the Tafileh WWTP
The U.S. Department of State, the Government of Jordan, and CDM Smith also made strides to accommodate the sanitation needs of Tafileh’s growing population by replacing the existing Tafileh WWTP with a higher-capacity, more efficient plant for residents of the Tafileh Governorate. The original WWTP was constructed in 1989 with enough capacity to receive 1,600 cubic meters of wastewater per day, but the new plant has allowed for waste processing capacity of 5,000 cubic meters per day with the potential to expand to 7,500 cubic meters per day. The new plant’s capacity tripled from about 25,000 to over 78,000 people. This treated wastewater serves as an alternative water source for agri­cul­tural irrigation, allowing potable surface and groundwater sources to be used for drinking.

## Providing freshwater wells in Dair Alla
CDM Smith is also supporting U.S. Department of State's Water and Wastewater Improvement Efforts for Dair Alla, a district in Balqa Governorate in the Jordan Valley with no wastewater pipeline networks, by providing well drilling contract tender evaluation and pre-contract services. To increase the availability of much-needed fresh water, the team is rehabilitating groundwater wells, upgrading a desalination water treatment plant and building a water transmission system serving 17 localities. These additions to Dair Alla will allow for an influx of fresh water available, keeping pace with the growing demand driven by population increases.
